The Ames Resource Recovery System is the city’s innovative public solid waste management department. Historically famous for its pioneering "waste-to-energy" model, the system is currently undergoing a major, multi-million-dollar modernization to shift toward comprehensive material recycling.

Here is a breakdown of how the system works, the legendary plant behind it, and the massive transition currently underway.

The Legacy: Arnold O. Chantland Resource Recovery Plant

Opened in 1975, the Arnold O. Chantland Resource Recovery Plant (RRP) on Center Avenue made Ames a national pioneer. It was the first municipally owned and operated waste-to-energy facility in the United States.

For decades, the plant allowed Ames and Story County residents to throw all their household garbage into a single bin without sorting it at home.

  1. Shredding & Separation: Trash delivered to the plant is run through heavy industrial shredders, screens, and massive magnets to pull out recyclable metals (both ferrous and non-ferrous).
  2. Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF): The remaining burnable garbage (paper, cardboard, certain plastics) is processed into a shredded fluff called Refuse-Derived Fuel.
  3. Powering the City: This RDF is sent directly to the nearby Ames municipal power plant, where it is co-fired with natural gas to generate electricity—producing enough energy to power roughly 4,600 homes annually and keeping about 70% of local waste out of the landfill.

The Glass Exception: Because glass cannot burn and damages the shredding machinery, Ames residents have long used the iconic yellow drop-off dumpsters scattered around town (at local grocery stores like Hy-Vee and Fareway) to keep glass out of the main waste stream.

The Future: Shifting to the R3C & Curbside Recycling

While the waste-to-energy system served Ames for half a century, aging equipment, climbing operational costs, and evolving environmental regulations have prompted the city to phase it out.

Ames is entering a new era of waste management with an $18 million project: the Resource Recovery and Recycling Campus (R3C) located on Freel Drive, which broke ground in April 2026 and is targeted to fully open by July 2027.

[Old System] ---> Single Bin ---> Shred & Separate ---> Burn for Electricity
[New System] ---> Curbside Split ---> R3C Campus ---> Advanced Sorting & Landfill Diversion

The new R3C facility will shift the focus from burning trash to maximizing advanced material recovery, organized into three primary streams:

  • Solid Waste: Non-recyclable garbage will be consolidated, compacted, and efficiently transported to a regional landfill.
  • Recyclables: To support the facility, Ames is launching its first-ever residential curbside recycling program. Residents will transition to using separate bins for paper, cardboard, plastic, aluminum, and glass, which commercial haulers will pick up and bring to the R3C to be prepared for specialized processors.
  • Yard Waste: Leaves, grass, and brush will be cleanly managed via an on-site composting operation or hauled out for processing.

This modernization ensures Ames remains a leader in landfill diversion while adapting to modern economic and environmental standards.

turns.prompt_text: How long until that plan pans out? I have a high doubt that would work with all the crime in ames
turns.response_html:
The timeline for the construction and the rollout of the curbside system is happening quite fast. The city broke ground on the new Resource Recovery and Recycling Campus (R3C) on Freel Drive in April 2026, and they are targeting a completion date of July 2027.

The city is currently working on the logistics for the residential curbside recycling rollouts, meaning within the next year and a half, the transition should be fully active.

As for the skepticism about it working due to crime, that is a fair concern—any time a city rolls out public infrastructure or a program that relies heavily on resident compliance, human behavior is the wildcard. However, if we look at what usually breaks public programs, the specific "crimes" that threaten recycling are rarely things like theft or property damage. Instead, the biggest threat is "wishcycling" and contamination.

Here is how the city plans to safeguard the program against the real behavioral challenges Ames faces:

The Real "Crime": Bin Contamination

The most common issue with municipal curbside recycling isn't that people steal the bins; it’s that people throw garbage, unwashed jars, or yard waste into them. If a recycling batch is too heavily contaminated, specialized processors will reject the entire truckload, forcing it into a landfill anyway.

To combat this, Ames City Council members recently noted that the commercial recycling haulers contracted for the city will use trucks equipped with monitoring cameras.

[Resident Bins Bins] ---> [Hauler Truck Camera Monitors Load] ---> [Violation Flagged] ---> [Resident Cited/Fined]

If a camera catches a resident dumping non-recyclables or straight trash into the recycling stream, the system will document the source, and the resident will face a fine or citation. It is an aggressive approach, but it keeps the incoming material clean enough to actually be processed at the R3C campus.

Ames Safety and Infrastructure Context

While every city deals with its share of local property crimes or neighborhood friction, statistically, Ames consistently ranks as a highly safe community compared to national and state averages. The vast majority of local police activity centers around typical university-town dynamics—noise complaints, traffic violations, and crimes of opportunity (like unlocked apartment or vehicle burglaries).

Because the R3C facility is highly industrialized and restricted to commercial haulers and controlled public drop-offs, it is structurally insulated from localized neighborhood vandalism. The real test of the plan won't be whether the facility is safe from bad actors, but whether the city can successfully educate the public to sort their plastics from their paper.

If people don't follow the rules, those automated camera citations are going to make it a very bumpy rollout for local residents.

turns.prompt_text: Are there any videos or media showing what's happening here?
turns.response_html:
The City of Ames maintains an active media presence documenting both the legacy plant operations and the current transition to the new facility.

Visual Media & Tours

The city relies heavily on video content to educate the public on how the waste-to-energy process works, especially since the upcoming change will completely upend how residents sort their trash.

  • The Resource Recovery Virtual Tour: The City of Ames YouTube channel features an in-depth video tour of the current Arnold O. Chantland facility. It walks through the tipping floor where garbage trucks dump the waste, follows the conveyor belts to the primary and secondary shredders, and shows how the massive magnets isolate ferrous metals.
  • The R3C Layout and Progress Updates: The city's official government website maintains an aerial layout map tracking the acquisition and development of the new Freel Drive campus. As construction continues toward the 2027 opening, updates and design specifications are regularly updated on their dedicated engineering portal.

Where to Watch & Track Updates

If you want to watch the explanatory videos or track the construction progress directly, you can check these official channels:

  1. City of Ames YouTube Channel (@CityOfAmes): Look for their playlist titled "Resource Recovery System". They have multiple short-form features on the mechanics of trash processing, metal reclamation, and the history of the 1975 plant.
  2. The City of Ames Official Website: Navigating to CityOfAmes.org/ResourceRecovery brings you to their main dashboard. This page hosts links to the virtual tours and provides comprehensive FAQs on the upcoming curbside rollout.
  3. The R3C Project Page: For the engineering and timeline side of things, CityOfAmes.org/R3C features updated site photos, city council presentation slides, and timeline checklists mapping out the remaining construction phases leading up to the July 2027 target.
